title: Cheryl Lerena
dek: The verse of David's mother — four poems, gathered from a writer's folder of books, short stories and competition entries.
living: **Cheryl Lerena is living.** This archive's rule for the living is **name only** — no dates, no places of residence, no photographs — and that rule is kept here. What is published is **her work**, at her son's request, and nothing about her life.
lead:
She is a **writer**, and the folder says so before a word is read: eight book projects, one of them redrafted **eleven times between 2005 and 2020**; a shelf of short stories; a **writers' group**, *The Write Company*, with its exercises and its **poetry competition**; a book club with its spreadsheets.

The poems were not all filed as poems. **One was buried inside a memorial address** — set as ordinary paragraphs in the middle of prose, in capitals, in a Word file from 2000, and nobody had ever taken it out and looked at it as verse. That is what this page is for.

**Four poems stand here.** A fifth is printed as uncertain. Two more are in Apple Pages format and cannot be read by this archive yet. And three pieces of verse in the folder are **not hers at all**, which matters as much as the ones that are.

poems.title: A poem for our grandchild
poems.occasion: Dated **13 August 2016** and signed at the head of the page — «A POEM FOR OUR GRANDCHILD **– by Cheryl Anne Defranceski**». The only piece in the whole folder where she names herself as the author of a poem. Written for a child not yet born.
text: We have not met you ….. yet
to see if you're a boy or girl
to count your fingers and your toes
and feel the softness of your nose
to touch your skin and hear your cries
and smell the sweetness of your flesh
to gaze deep in your eyes
and whisper softly in your ears
our endless love for you always
And as we wait with bated breath
for you who we have not yet met
sleep well sweet child until it's time
for you to safely leave the womb
We wait for you with bated breath …..
poems.note: Fifteen lines that never once say *I*. It is **«we»** all the way through, and the refrain — *waiting with bated breath* — opens the poem, turns it, and closes it. Almost every line is a **sense**: touch, hearing, smell, sight. A poem about a person who does not exist yet, written entirely out of what it will be like to have a body near you.

poems.title: I had a darling sister
poems.occasion: Written for the **first anniversary** of her sister's death and read to the family. **Catherine Tersia Lerena, called Rene, 21 May 1952 – 30 September 1999.** It stands inside the memorial address, not set apart as verse.
poems.conf: doc — signed at the foot of the document it stands in
text: A dream her life was not
She knew pain as her friend
poems.note: Nine lines, no rhyme, and it ends on an ellipsis rather than a full stop — the same trailing dots she uses all through the prose around it, as though the sentence could not be finished. **«She knew pain as her friend»** is the line it turns on. It is not a comfort and it does not try to be.

poems.title: Two sides
poems.conf: doc — in her folder, in her voice, undisputed
text: That life has not one but two sides
Then the dark cold of night
That life has not one but two sides
Hear the laughter loud and clear
That life has not one but two sides
Taste the words of kindness and love
Spit out the words of lies and hate
That life has not one but two sides
Smell the sweetness of a rose
and the stench of a titan arum
That life has not one but two sides
To the tale of two sides
To the tale of two sides
poems.note: The most **built** thing she wrote. A refrain — *open your eyes and behold that life has not one but two sides* — repeated five times, and behind it a structure she never announces: **the five senses in order**. Sight, then hearing, then taste, then smell, then touch. And the fifth stanza reaches past the obvious for its stink — not a drain, not rot, but a **titan arum**, the corpse flower, which is a deliberate choice by somebody who went looking. The closing turn swaps *eyes* for **ears**.

poems.title: A heart breaks
poems.conf: doc — in her folder, in her voice, undisputed
poems.note: Seventeen lines, none longer than four words. It runs a **single night into a single day and back to sunset**, and the only thing that develops is the pain: it *eats*, and then it **feasts**. The verbs do all the work, and the heart is never *hers* — never *my* heart, always *a* heart.

poems.title: If love could change the way things are
poems.occasion: Stands a few paragraphs below «I had a darling sister», in the same memorial address.
text: If love could change the way things are
You would live forever and go so far
You'd know that I am always there
That I'll always love you, I'll always care
poems.note: Four lines, rhymed **aabb**, sitting immediately before the sentence *«In October of 1992 a card arrived in the mail … here it is, I will share it with you»*. So it may be hers, or it may be **the verse off that card**. The document does not say, and this archive will not decide for it. **Printed as uncertain rather than claimed as hers or dropped for being awkward.**

excluded.heading: Two poems that are not hers, and are not printed
excluded.text:
**«Life is a sojourn here on earth»** sits in a letter she wrote to her surviving sister in **November 1999**, six weeks after Rene died. It is by **Helen Steiner Rice**, the American writer of devotional verse whose poems went out on greeting cards by the million — almost certainly how it reached a Johannesburg letterbox. **In copyright. Not printed.**

**«Each day I love you more, today more than yesterday and less than tomorrow»** is a single line kept in the Poems folder. It is a translation of **Rosemonde Gérard**, *L'éternelle chanson*, 1889 — *«chaque jour je t'aime davantage, aujourd'hui plus qu'hier et bien moins que demain»* — one of the most quoted lines in French. **Not hers either.**

Both are named rather than dropped in silence, because **a woman keeping a poem she loves is not the author of it**, and an archive that prints everything in a folder ends up attributing greeting cards to grieving people.

rest.heading: What else is in the folder, and why none of it is here
rest.text:
The poems are the smallest part of it. Also in the folder: **eight book projects** — *My Love Story*, redrafted eleven times from 2005 to 2020; *Husky*; *Soul Mates*; *A Murder*; *Desperate End*, whose first chapter was written for a creative-writing course and carries her name on the title; *Infidelity*; *Insanity*. Around **fifteen short stories**. Personal essays. A **writers' group** file thick with exercises, character sketches and competition entries.

**None of it is published**, and none of it is quoted here.

And a warning that has to be given plainly. **Several files in the Poems folder are not poems.** They are private prose, and some of it is about named living people — including her son — written in distress and never meant for a website. This archive has read them only far enough to know they are not verse, and has **published nothing from them, quoted nothing from them, and will not.**

If more of the writing is to appear, **it is Cheryl's to release, piece by piece.** This page will take whatever she gives it.

source: From the family's own writing folder, read 10 September 2026 at David's request. Poems transcribed exactly: line breaks, spelling, and the trailing ellipses are hers and are not corrected. «I had a darling sister» and «If love could change the way things are» come from the memorial address for Catherine Tersia Lerena, first anniversary, September 2000. Attributions for the two excluded poems: Helen Steiner Rice, and Rosemonde Gérard's «L'éternelle chanson», 1889.

pending.heading: Two more, which this archive cannot open
pending.text:
**«Corona virus poem»** and **«Gratefulness for 1 year»** are saved in **Apple Pages** format, whose text is compressed inside a binary the archive cannot reliably decode. Fragments surface — *«Faster and f…»*, *«Like a rocket bl…»*, *«Out of control»* for the first; *«Gratitude is at…»*, *«Believe, recei…»* for the second — and no more.

**They need thirty seconds and an export to Word or PDF**, and then they belong on this page.
